en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Four Houses:
When the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the West, he did not rely on words and letters; he pointed directly at the human mind, so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Mind-to-mind, they transmitted the seal down to the Sixth Patriarch. From the Sixth Patriarch downward, the lineage divided into the Nanyue and Qingyuan lines, of which Nanyue was the most prominent.
The Linji school further branched into the Linji and Guiyang traditions, of which Linji was the most flourishing.

The *Recorded Sayings* (Yulu) of the four masters transmitted by the orthodox lineage—namely the four venerable patriarchs Mazu, Baizhang, Huangbo, and Linji following Nanyue—are the words with which they responded to the capacities of others and guided sentient beings.
These range from ten thousand words at the longest to no fewer than several thousand words at the shortest; they are truly texts.

Is it not so? Is it not the very essence of words? Is the meaning of the West’s arrival truly nothing other than this? Alas! To point at the moon to show the way to the deluded, the deluded see only the finger and miss the moon;
to use a basin to illustrate the sun, the blind person grasps only the bell of the basin. Such are the various distinctions.
How can words ever suffice? Can those venerable masters truly forget words? Is it not that they wish to point directly to the human mind so that one may achieve sudden awakening?
It is like painting a portrait: seeking the likeness through form, one achieves only an elevenfold resemblance. Only this wondrous luminosity [is beyond description].
It cannot be sought through form; it cannot be measured by the mind. How much less can it be expressed in words?

Even if it could be expressed, were one to enter through the gate, I fear it would not be the family treasure. To clarify it through words is not to depart from hearsay. O Venerable Elders, can you endure direct speech?
If you cannot endure direct speech, it is difficult to speak; yet you cannot forget words either. Such is the state of the minds of the Venerable Elders.
"What is to be done? Some may say: "A person possesses this mind and naturally has its own capacity for discernment and awakening; why trouble oneself with the prolixity of various venerable elders?
One does not realize that as desire begins to sprout, false knowledge emerges alongside it. One discriminates among external objects and mistakenly deems them wondrously luminous.

Thus one pursues the delusive while turning one's back on the Real, seeking further and further away from it. Should one cling to fixed characteristics, one will immediately fall into a black mountain ghost cave. Listen to this [instruction]:...
Grass. Furthermore, as people have come to encroach upon the harvests of others and the lineage of transmission has grown distant, the remaining traces are vast and obscure.
Without authoritative maxims, how can one seek the true pulse of the Dharma? Master Fufu Xinyi entered deeply into samādhi and was wondrously liberated from verbal expression;

he attained profound resonance with various venerable elders. He maintained that for those entering the Way, there is no other step to ascend; and for those bestowing the Dharma, there is no better medium than woodblocks to propagate it widely. Thus, [he compiled this work].

Dong’an’s Master Jingshan Ning has long cultivated the roots of spiritual awakening and deeply nurtured the power of goodness. Together with others, he has donated his funds to complete the carving of this work.
Fearing that viewers might become mired in the mere words and letters, Master Xin has requested that I compose a preface to clarify its underlying intent.
I cannot deeply fathom the minds of the various venerable elders. I have heard the teachings of the Sage, which say: "I wish to remain without words.
Yet, for those today who aspire to emulate the Sage, if they set aside the Sage’s words, how else could they recognize him? One must know that true mastery lies in skillful understanding.
Vast and unceasing, it is all one silence. For those who do not understand well, it lies beyond words and cuts off all phrases, remaining separated by ten thousand worldly dusts.
As for the words of these four venerable elders—were they mere letters and words, or were they not? Were they a direct pointing, or were they not a direct pointing?
Surely there must be those capable of discerning this. Written by Tang Hezheng of Biling.

After I had finished editing and publishing this collection of the records of four masters, a guest questioned me, saying, "If it merely takes the form of written words, it belongs to verbal teaching (*yanjiao*).
How can it be called the 'Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings' (*jiaowai biedian*)? I replied, "Not so. While words are certainly teaching, the absence of words is likewise [teaching]."

This is the teaching. Even such statements as "it is not existence," "it is not non-existence," "it is not neither existence nor non-existence," and "it is not neither non-existence nor non-non-existence" are all teachings.
This is what is meant by "transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations. The guest further said: "When a sacred tortoise drags its tail, its tracks become even more prominent.
Are not the words of these four venerable masters not likewise like dragging a tail? I replied: "No. It is not so. Regarding the words of the four venerable masters..."
To obliterate traces with intention is not "outside the teachings. To obliterate traces without intention is also not "outside the teachings.
Even to be neither with intention nor without intention, neither not with intention nor not without intention—to possess such non-intentionality is also not "outside the teachings. The guest said:
If that is so, who would say this is a "separate transmission"? I say: wait until you have thoroughly penetrated the following text, and then I shall try to tell you.
On the first day of the eighth month of the autumn in the Dingwei year of the Wanli era, written by the monk Zhengzhuan of Jingxi as a postscript to the engraved records of the four masters.
A visitor showed me a collection of recorded sayings from four masters. I recited it all day long, unable to let go of it. Consequently, I brought it out to read with Master Yixin.
The Master requested that it be carved into printing blocks. I said, "The recorded sayings from various quarters are already widely circulated;
why must you further indulge in such an undertaking? The Master replied, "Not so. Generally speaking, the speech of our ancestral house is..."

The essential point requires wondrous awakening; it admits of no deliberation or conjecture. It is intended for one to attain thorough penetration upon taking a stand, to realize it immediately in this very moment.
Why then attempt to set it forth in written proclamations? Would that not only increase the tangle of complications? Would it not be like stirring up dust with the wind to blind people’s eyes?
Furthermore, when exerting the great pivot and manifesting the great function, how can this compare to the most earnest, grandmotherly compassion of Mazu and Huangbo?
As for how one receives and transmits [the Dharma], the manner in which Baizhang and Linji display their teachings is particularly extraordinary.
How could I bear to leave such matters unexamined, failing to bring them forth so as to provide a sense of liberation for all ages? I said:
"Does the Master wish to seize another's nostrils to make them feel pain? Or do you intend to strike the assembly with your staff, wishing for me to throw a punch in return? The Master laughed and—
There was no reply. I therefore invited these eminent gentlemen to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and donated my stipend to have this work carved for publication.
It is my hope that those who apply their minds to this Way may find their restless seeking suddenly stilled, so that they may realize their return to the source in silent stillness.
That you four venerable seniors could meet together is indeed a rare occurrence once in a thousand years. Your Master’s encouragement of this carving will surely provide more than a small benefit.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month in the Jichou year of the Wanli era, recorded by the Layman Xie Ning of Anjing, Dongshan.
